name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q01 - Physiological roles of major plasma proteins

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding plasma proteins and plasma constituents:

Column I (Plasma Protein / Component) Column II (Primary Function or Definition)
(A) Fibrinogen(I) Maintenance of osmotic balance
(B) Globulins(II) Plasma lacking coagulation factors
(C) Albumins(III) Clotting or coagulation of blood
(D) Serum(IV) Defense mechanisms of the body

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen is a high-molecular-weight soluble plasma protein synthesized by the liver. Upon activation during hemostasis, it is converted into insoluble fibrin threads that form a meshwork trapping blood cells, thereby facilitating the clotting or coagulation of blood.

Step 2: Role of Globulins
Globulins are a diverse group of serum proteins comprising immunoglobulins (antibodies) and transport proteins that are primarily involved in defense mechanisms of the body against infectious agents.

Step 3: Role of Albumins
Albumins constitute approximately 60 percent of total plasma proteins and are the major determinants of plasma oncotic pressure, playing an indispensable role in the maintenance of osmotic balance between vascular and tissue spaces.

Step 4: Definition of Serum
Serum represents the liquid fraction of blood that remains after whole blood is allowed to clot; it is identical in solute composition to plasma but completely lacks fibrinogen and other coagulation factors.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Fibrinogen corresponds to clotting or coagulation of blood; Globulins correspond to defense mechanisms of the body; Albumins correspond to maintenance of osmotic balance; and Serum corresponds to plasma lacking coagulation factors.

Final Answer: Fibrinogen pairs with clotting or coagulation of blood; Globulins pair with defense mechanisms of the body; Albumins pair with maintenance of osmotic balance; Serum pairs with plasma lacking coagulation factors.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q02 - Functional characteristics of human leukocyte types

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding human leukocytes and their specialized functions:

Column I (Leukocyte Type) Column II (Functional Role or Characteristic)
(A) Neutrophils(I) Secrete histamine and heparin in inflammatory reactions
(B) Basophils(II) Specialized cells responsible for immune responses
(C) Eosinophils(III) Most abundant phagocytic white blood cells
(D) Lymphocytes(IV) Resist infections and associated with allergic reactions

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Functional Role of Neutrophils
Neutrophils are polymorphonuclear granulocytes constituting 60 to 65 percent of circulating leukocytes, functioning as the primary phagocytic responders that ingest invading pathogens.

Step 2: Functional Role of Basophils
Basophils represent 0.5 to 1 percent of white blood cells and synthesize and release inflammatory mediators, including histamine, serotonin, and the anticoagulant heparin.

Step 3: Functional Role of Eosinophils
Eosinophils comprise 2 to 3 percent of leukocytes, containing hydrolytic granules specialized to combat parasitic infestations and participate in hypersensitivity and allergic reactions.

Step 4: Functional Role of Lymphocytes
Lymphocytes constitute 20 to 25 percent of white blood cells and differentiate into B and T cells that orchestrate antigen-specific adaptive immune responses.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Neutrophils correspond to most abundant phagocytic white blood cells; Basophils correspond to secreting histamine and heparin in inflammatory reactions; Eosinophils correspond to resisting infections and allergic reactions; and Lymphocytes correspond to immune responses.

Final Answer: Neutrophils pair with most abundant phagocytic white blood cells; Basophils pair with secreting histamine and heparin in inflammatory reactions; Eosinophils pair with resisting infections and allergic reactions; Lymphocytes pair with specialized cells responsible for immune responses.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q03 - Antigen and antibody distribution in blood

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding ABO blood groups and their immunological markers:

Column I (ABO Blood Group) Column II (Antigens on Erythrocytes and Antibodies in Plasma)
(A) Blood group A(I) Carries both surface antigens A and B on RBCs and no antibodies in plasma
(B) Blood group B(II) Lacks surface antigens on RBCs and carries both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma
(C) Blood group AB(III) Carries antigen B on RBCs and anti-A antibodies in plasma
(D) Blood group O(IV) Carries antigen A on RBCs and anti-B antibodies in plasma

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Immunological Features of Group A
Individuals classified under blood group A express surface agglutinogen A on their red blood cell membranes and possess naturally occurring anti-B isoantibodies in their plasma.

Step 2: Immunological Features of Group B
Individuals of blood group B exhibit surface agglutinogen B on their erythrocytes and produce circulating anti-A isoantibodies in their plasma.

Step 3: Immunological Features of Group AB
Erythrocytes of group AB individuals express both surface antigen A and antigen B, but their plasma is devoid of both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, making them universal plasma recipients.

Step 4: Immunological Features of Group O
Group O individuals do not express surface antigen A or antigen B on their erythrocytes, while their circulating plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, rendering them universal erythrocyte donors.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Blood group A corresponds to antigen A on RBCs and anti-B antibodies in plasma; Blood group B corresponds to antigen B on RBCs and anti-A antibodies in plasma; Blood group AB corresponds to both antigens on RBCs and no antibodies in plasma; and Blood group O corresponds to no surface antigens on RBCs and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma.

Final Answer: Blood group A pairs with antigen A on RBCs and anti-B antibodies in plasma; Blood group B pairs with antigen B on RBCs and anti-A antibodies in plasma; Blood group AB pairs with both antigens A and B on RBCs and no antibodies in plasma; Blood group O pairs with lack of surface antigens on RBCs and presence of both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q04 - Biochemical components of blood coagulation cascade

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding the biochemical factors involved in the blood coagulation cascade:

Column I (Clotting Factor or Component) Column II (Biochemical Role in Hemostasis)
(A) Thrombokinase(I) Inactive plasma protein converted into active thrombin
(B) Prothrombin(II) Soluble plasma precursor cleaved to yield insoluble fibrin mesh
(C) Fibrinogen(III) Essential mineral cofactor required at multiple clotting steps
(D) Calcium ions(IV) Enzymatic complex generated by cascade of linked reactions

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Biochemical Action of Thrombokinase
Thrombokinase is a multi-molecular enzymatic complex assembled through an extrinsic and intrinsic cascade of plasma and platelet factors following tissue trauma, serving to cleave prothrombin.

Step 2: Biochemical Action of Prothrombin
Prothrombin is an inactive circulating plasma zymogen that undergoes proteolytic activation by thrombokinase to yield active thrombin.

Step 3: Biochemical Action of Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen is a large soluble plasma protein that is enzymatically cleaved by thrombin into fibrin monomers, which polymerize to create a stable insoluble fibrillar meshwork.

Step 4: Biochemical Action of Calcium Ions
Divalent calcium ions act as an essential cofactor facilitating prothrombinase assembly, tenase activation, and fibrin cross-linking throughout the hemostatic cascade.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Thrombokinase corresponds to the enzymatic complex generated by cascade; Prothrombin corresponds to the inactive protein converted into thrombin; Fibrinogen corresponds to the soluble precursor cleaved to form fibrin mesh; and Calcium ions correspond to the essential mineral cofactor.

Final Answer: Thrombokinase pairs with enzymatic complex generated by cascade of linked reactions; Prothrombin pairs with inactive plasma protein converted into active thrombin; Fibrinogen pairs with soluble plasma precursor cleaved to yield insoluble fibrin mesh; Calcium ions pair with essential mineral cofactor required at multiple clotting steps.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q05 - Vertebrate classes and heart chamber patterns

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding vertebrate heart anatomy and circulatory patterns:

Column I (Vertebrate Group) Column II (Cardiac Architecture and Flow Pathway)
(A) Fishes(I) Four-chambered heart in a reptilian exception
(B) Amphibians(II) Four-chambered heart with complete double circulation
(C) Crocodiles(III) Two-chambered heart with single circulation
(D) Birds and mammals(IV) Three-chambered heart with incomplete double circulation

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Circulatory System of Fishes
Fishes feature a two-chambered heart comprising a single atrium and a single ventricle; deoxygenated blood pumped by the ventricle undergoes gill oxygenation and flows directly to tissues before returning, representing single circulation.

Step 2: Circulatory System of Amphibians
Amphibians possess a three-chambered heart with two atria and one common ventricle, where oxygenated pulmonary blood and deoxygenated systemic blood enter separately but mix prior to ejection, producing incomplete double circulation.

Step 3: Circulatory System of Crocodiles
Crocodilians depart from typical reptilian cardiac anatomy by possessing a completely partitioned four-chambered heart containing two atria and two ventricles.

Step 4: Circulatory System of Birds and Mammals
Birds and mammals possess fully separated four-chambered hearts with two atria and two ventricles, completely isolating pulmonary and systemic vascular circuits in true double circulation.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Fishes correspond to a two-chambered heart with single circulation; Amphibians correspond to a three-chambered heart with incomplete double circulation; Crocodiles correspond to a four-chambered heart in a reptilian exception; and Birds and mammals correspond to a four-chambered heart with complete double circulation.

Final Answer: Fishes pair with two-chambered heart with single circulation; Amphibians pair with three-chambered heart with incomplete double circulation; Crocodiles pair with four-chambered heart in a reptilian exception; Birds and mammals pair with four-chambered heart with complete double circulation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q06 - Anatomical positions of human cardiac valves

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding the internal anatomy and valve locations of the human heart:

Column I (Cardiac Valve) Column II (Anatomical Aperture Guarded by Valve)
(A) Tricuspid valve(I) Opening between left atrium and left ventricle
(B) Bicuspid valve(II) Opening between right ventricle and pulmonary artery
(C) Aortic semilunar valve(III) Opening between right atrium and right ventricle
(D) Pulmonary semilunar valve(IV) Opening between left ventricle and systemic aorta

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomy of the Tricuspid Valve
The right atrioventricular opening is guarded by a valve formed of three fibrous cusps, designated the tricuspid valve, ensuring forward flow into the right ventricle.

Step 2: Anatomy of the Bicuspid Valve
The left atrioventricular opening is protected by a two-cusped structure designated the bicuspid or mitral valve, preventing backward flow into the left atrium during ventricular contraction.

Step 3: Anatomy of the Aortic Semilunar Valve
The exit of the left ventricle into the systemic aorta is guarded by pocket-like aortic semilunar cusps that close during ventricular diastole.

Step 4: Anatomy of the Pulmonary Semilunar Valve
The outlet of the right ventricle leading into the pulmonary trunk is guarded by pulmonary semilunar valves that prevent regurgitation of blood from pulmonary circulation.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Tricuspid valve corresponds to opening between right atrium and right ventricle; Bicuspid valve corresponds to opening between left atrium and left ventricle; Aortic semilunar valve corresponds to opening between left ventricle and systemic aorta; and Pulmonary semilunar valve corresponds to opening between right ventricle and pulmonary artery.

Final Answer: Tricuspid valve pairs with opening between right atrium and right ventricle; Bicuspid valve pairs with opening between left atrium and left ventricle; Aortic semilunar valve pairs with opening between left ventricle and systemic aorta; Pulmonary semilunar valve pairs with opening between right ventricle and pulmonary artery.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q07 - Electrical phases of a standard electrocardiogram

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding waveforms of a standard electrocardiogram and their underlying cardiac events:

Column I (ECG Deflection) Column II (Underlying Electrophysiological Event)
(A) P-wave(I) Ventricular repolarisation returning musculature to resting state
(B) QRS complex(II) Marks the clinical conclusion of ventricular systole
(C) T-wave(III) Depolarisation of ventricles initiating ventricular systole
(D) End of T-wave(IV) Depolarisation of atria leading to atrial contraction

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrophysiology of the P-wave
The P-wave is the first positive deflection on an electrocardiogram, representing the wave of electrical excitation or depolarization sweeping across both atria, which initiates atrial systole.

Step 2: Electrophysiology of the QRS Complex
The QRS complex represents rapid electrical depolarization across the ventricular myocardium, marking the onset of ventricular systole shortly after the Q wave.

Step 3: Electrophysiology of the T-wave
The T-wave is an upward deflection representing ventricular repolarization, during which ventricular myocytes recover from an excited state back to their resting membrane potential.

Step 4: Clinical Significance of the End of T-wave
The terminal baseline transition at the end of the T-wave marks the cessation of ventricular electrical repolarization and the conclusion of ventricular mechanical systole.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
P-wave corresponds to depolarisation of atria; QRS complex corresponds to depolarisation of ventricles; T-wave corresponds to ventricular repolarisation; and End of T-wave corresponds to marks the clinical conclusion of ventricular systole.

Final Answer: P-wave pairs with depolarisation of atria leading to atrial contraction; QRS complex pairs with depolarisation of ventricles initiating ventricular systole; T-wave pairs with ventricular repolarisation returning musculature to resting state; End of T-wave pairs with marks the clinical conclusion of ventricular systole.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q08 - Components of the human cardiac conduction system

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding the specialized nodal tissues of the cardiac conduction system:

Column I (Conducting System Element) Column II (Anatomical Location and Conducting Function)
(A) Sino-atrial node(I) Lower left corner of right atrium near atrioventricular septum
(B) Atrio-ventricular node(II) Crosses fibrous septum and divides atop interventricular septum into bundle branches
(C) Atrio-ventricular bundle(III) Minute terminal conducting arborizations distributed throughout ventricular myocardium
(D) Purkinje fibres(IV) Right upper corner of right atrium, generates 70-75 action potentials per minute

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of the Sino-atrial Node
The sino-atrial node sits in the right upper wall of the right atrium; it possesses the highest intrinsic automaticity, discharging 70 to 75 action potentials per minute to serve as the cardiac pacemaker.

Step 2: Role of the Atrio-ventricular Node
The atrio-ventricular node is positioned in the lower left corner of the right atrium adjacent to the fibrous atrioventricular septum, relaying incoming atrial excitation toward the ventricles.

Step 3: Role of the Atrio-ventricular Bundle
The atrio-ventricular bundle (bundle of His) penetrates the fibrous atrioventricular ring, emerges on the crest of the interventricular septum, and bifurcates into right and left bundle branches.

Step 4: Role of the Purkinje Fibres
Purkinje fibres arise from the bundle branches and form a fine subendocardial arborization throughout both ventricular myocardial walls, propagating impulses rapidly for coordinated contraction.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Sino-atrial node corresponds to generating 70-75 action potentials in right upper atrium; Atrio-ventricular node corresponds to lower left right atrium; Atrio-ventricular bundle corresponds to crossing septum and dividing; and Purkinje fibres correspond to minute arborizations in ventricular walls.

Final Answer: Sino-atrial node pairs with right upper corner of right atrium, generates 70-75 action potentials per minute; Atrio-ventricular node pairs with lower left corner of right atrium near atrioventricular septum; Atrio-ventricular bundle pairs with crosses fibrous septum and divides atop interventricular septum into bundle branches; Purkinje fibres pair with minute terminal conducting arborizations distributed throughout ventricular myocardium.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q09 - Vascular circuits and histological vessel layers

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding blood vessel histology, specialized portal systems, and circulatory circuits:

Column I (Circulatory Component) Column II (Histological or Anatomical Feature)
(A) Hepatic portal vein(I) Dedicated vascular network exclusively supplying and draining cardiac muscle
(B) Coronary circulation(II) Middle vascular coat with smooth muscle and elastic fibers, thinner in veins
(C) Tunica media(III) Carries nutrient-rich blood from digestive tract to liver before systemic return
(D) Tunica intima(IV) Innermost vascular coat consisting of simple squamous endothelium

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of the Hepatic Portal Vein
The hepatic portal system forms a unique venous bypass wherein the hepatic portal vein collects deoxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from gastrointestinal viscera and routes it directly to liver sinusoids prior to caval delivery.

Step 2: Role of Coronary Circulation
Because heart muscle has immense metabolic demands, it is nourished by an exclusive coronary arterial and venous system that supplies and drains blood from the myocardium.

Step 3: Histology of Tunica Media
The tunica media constitutes the intermediate vascular layer made of circularly arranged smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers, being significantly thinner in veins than in systemic arteries.

Step 4: Histology of Tunica Intima
The tunica intima is the innermost tunic of the blood vessel wall, formed by a delicate single layer of squamous endothelium that provides a smooth, non-thrombogenic surface for blood flow.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Hepatic portal vein corresponds to carrying blood from digestive tract to liver; Coronary circulation corresponds to dedicated network supplying cardiac muscle; Tunica media corresponds to middle smooth muscle coat thinner in veins; and Tunica intima corresponds to innermost squamous endothelium.

Final Answer: Hepatic portal vein pairs with carries nutrient-rich blood from digestive tract to liver before systemic return; Coronary circulation pairs with dedicated vascular network exclusively supplying and draining cardiac muscle; Tunica media pairs with middle vascular coat with smooth muscle and elastic fibers, thinner in veins; Tunica intima pairs with innermost vascular coat consisting of simple squamous endothelium.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MATCH_LIST_Q10 - Clinical features of human cardiovascular disorders

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column I with their corresponding descriptions in Column II regarding etiologies and manifestations of human circulatory disorders:

Column I (Circulatory Disorder) Column II (Diagnostic Hallmark and Clinical Manifestation)
(A) Hypertension(I) State wherein the heart does not pump blood effectively to meet bodily needs
(B) Atherosclerosis(II) Severe chest pain appearing when insufficient oxygen reaches heart muscle
(C) Angina pectoris(III) Repeated arterial blood pressure readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher
(D) Heart failure(IV) Lumen of coronary arteries narrowed by deposits of calcium, fat, and fibrous tissue

Select the correct match from the options given:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Clinical Features of Hypertension
Hypertension is diagnosed when multiple resting sphygmomanometer readings show systolic pressures of 140 mm Hg or higher and diastolic pressures of 90 mm Hg or higher, straining vital organ perfusion.

Step 2: Clinical Features of Atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis (coronary artery disease) involves the progressive accumulation of atheromatous plaques containing cholesterol, lipids, calcium, and fibrous connective tissue within coronary arteries, constricting their lumen.

Step 3: Clinical Features of Angina Pectoris
Angina pectoris presents with episodes of acute thoracic chest pain caused by transient myocardial ischemia when coronary flow fails to deliver sufficient oxygen to meet myocardial demand.

Step 4: Clinical Features of Heart Failure
Heart failure describes a functional deficit in which cardiac ventricles fail to generate sufficient forward stroke volume and cardiac output to satisfy metabolic demands of peripheral tissues, commonly causing pulmonary venous congestion.

Step 5: Synthesis of Correct Associations
Hypertension corresponds to blood pressure readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher; Atherosclerosis corresponds to arterial lumen narrowed by lipid and calcium deposits; Angina pectoris corresponds to severe chest pain from insufficient oxygen delivery; and Heart failure corresponds to inability of heart to pump blood effectively to meet bodily needs.

Final Answer: Hypertension pairs with repeated arterial blood pressure readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher; Atherosclerosis pairs with lumen of coronary arteries narrowed by deposits of calcium, fat, and fibrous tissue; Angina pectoris pairs with severe chest pain appearing when insufficient oxygen reaches heart muscle; Heart failure pairs with state wherein the heart does not pump blood effectively to meet bodily needs.
